w: What's tested The spleen and the thymus, which the course's learning objectives name: their histologic regions, what fills each region and what each organ does (white pulp, PALS, marginal zone and red pulp; thymic cortex, medulla, blood-thymus barrier and T cell education) Telling the blood cells apart by their described features and jobs: neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, monocytes and lymphocytes, red cells and platelets, and how common each white cell is The three lymphocyte classes: B cells (surface IgM and IgD, plasma cells), helper and cytotoxic T cells (CD4 with MHC II, CD8 with MHC I) and NK cells (no B or T markers, ADCC) Innate versus adaptive immunity, and what belongs to each Primary versus secondary lymphoid organs, and where the B and T cells sit in each one Lymph nodes, MALT and Peyer's patches with their M cells, and the tonsils of Waldeyer's ring Dr. Herr, the course director, gives Lecture 19, Introduction to Hematology, on Tuesday, November 17, at 1 pm. His deck opens the hematology block in two halves: the cells of the blood and what each one does, then the lymphoid organs and tissues (bone marrow, thymus, lymph nodes, MALT, tonsils and spleen), their histology, and where the B and T cells live in each. His slides carry full speaker notes, and these notes fold them in as what he is likely to say. These notes are from the slides; the lecture is Tuesday, and they will be checked against its recording. His objectives: tell the blood cells apart and say what each does; know what the lymphoid organs do, which are primary or secondary, their histology, and where the B and T cells sit in each. The course objectives name the spleen and the thymus. On Exam 2 he said he would not test stained images, only drawings, so these notes describe each cell and region by its features. The cells of the blood Blood holds three kinds of cells. The erythrocytes, the red blood cells, make up about 99 percent of the cells in the blood, and they carry oxygen and carbon dioxide. The platelets are fragments of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow, and they initiate blood clotting. The rest are the white blood cells, or leukocytes: two classes, five types. The granulocytes have prominent granules in their cytoplasm and play a role in innate immunity. They are the neutrophils, the eosinophils and the basophils. The agranulocytes lack those granules: the monocytes and the lymphocytes, which are the B cells, T cells and NK cells. How common each white cell is follows a fixed order, and his slides give the shares: neutrophils 50 to 70 percent, lymphocytes 30 to 40 percent, monocytes 2 to 8 percent, eosinophils 1 to 4 percent, and basophils under 1 percent. A memory cue for the order, most to least common: Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas (neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils). Where the blood cells come from His hematopoiesis figure starts from one pluripotential stem cell, which gives rise to two multipotential stem cells. The lymphoid multipotential stem cell makes the lymphocyte colony-forming cells, which become the B and T lymphocytes. The myeloid multipotential stem cell makes the colony-forming cells for the erythrocytes, for the megakaryocytes, which develop into the platelets, and for the granulocytes and monocytes. So a monocyte is a myeloid cell even though it has no prominent granules, and the lymphocytes are the lymphoid line. In an adult, every one of these cells comes from the bone marrow: the T and B lymphocytes, the mononuclear phagocytes, the platelets, the erythrocytes and the other leukocytes. Innate and adaptive immunity The cells of the immune system take part in two kinds of immunity. Nonspecific, or innate, immunity is the set of pre-existing defenses against microbial invasion, in place before any contact. It has five parts: physical barriers, the skin and mucous membranes; chemical defenses, such as a low pH; secretory substances, such as lysozyme, thiocyanate in saliva and interferons; phagocytic cells, the macrophages, neutrophils and monocytes; and the natural killer (NK) cells. Specific, or adaptive, immunity produces acquired resistance. A first contact with a specific antigen or foreign agent starts a chain of reactions carried out by the effector B and T cells, and it often leaves a state of immune memory. It has two arms. The humoral response belongs to the B cells: they make antibodies, which mark invaders for destruction by other cells. The cellular immune response belongs to the T cells: it targets transformed cells and virus-infected cells for destruction by killer (cytotoxic) T cells. Thiocyanate in saliva is the dentist's entry on his innate list. His slide also puts "(Killer T cells)" after natural killer cells. NK cells are not T cells: his own NK slide says they lack B and T cell markers. The killer T cells are the cytotoxic, CD8-positive T cells of adaptive immunity. Neutrophils Neutrophils are the main phagocyte of the blood, 50 to 70 percent of the white cells, and the body's first line of defense against bacteria. They are highly motile. They circulate in the blood for about 10 hours, then migrate into the tissues. To recognize one by its features: a multi-lobed nucleus, large stores of glycogen with few mitochondria, and two types of granules. The primary granules contain elastase and myeloperoxidase. The other, secondary granules contain lysozyme and proteases. His summary table gives their job in one line: they phagocytose and destroy invading bacteria. His slide labels the secondary granules "Azur granules". Histology texts (Junqueira, Ross) call the primary granules the azurophilic ones and the secondary granules the specific granules. The safe thing to learn is the contents: elastase and myeloperoxidase in the primary granules. Eosinophils Eosinophils are 1 to 4 percent of the white cells. Their features: a large bilobed nucleus and large specific granules that stain red, or pink, with eosin, the dye they are named for. Their granules hold two weapons. Peroxidase binds to microorganisms and helps kill them. Major basic protein, MBP, also called PRG2, binds to and disrupts the membranes of parasites, both protozoa and helminths (worms), and it also makes basophils release histamine. Eosinophils accumulate in the blood and tissues in parasitic infections, and their numbers rise in allergic reactions such as hay fever. They carry surface receptors for IgE, the antibody seen mainly in allergic responses. His table: they destroy larger parasites and modulate allergic responses. Basophils Basophils are the rarest white cell, under 1 percent. The nucleus is typically bilobed, and the large specific granules stain dark blue or purple. The granules contain heparin and vasoactive substances; his table says basophils release histamine in certain immune reactions. Basophils also carry IgE receptors. When IgE binds them, the basophil releases its vasoactive contents. Basophils play a prominent role in bronchial asthma. Eosinophils and basophils both have a bilobed nucleus and IgE receptors. Tell them apart by the granules: red with eosin (the eosinophil: peroxidase and major basic protein, parasites and allergy) or dark blue to purple (the basophil: heparin and histamine, asthma). Monocytes Monocytes are 2 to 8 percent of the white cells. They are fairly large cells with a single nucleus that is often indented or horseshoe-shaped, and they have prominent lysosomes. They circulate for about 3 days. During inflammation they migrate into the tissues, where they differentiate into macrophages; together the monocytes and macrophages make up the mononuclear phagocytic system. They phagocytose bacteria, cells and tissue debris, and they express MHC class II molecules, which is how a macrophage presents antigen to helper T cells. Lymphocytes Lymphocytes are 30 to 40 percent of the white cells. They come in two sizes: the large ones, about 9 to 12 micrometers, are the NK cells, and the small ones, about 6 to 8 micrometers, are the B and T cells. A lymphocyte has a spherical, slightly indented nucleus, and its light-staining cytoplasm is only a thin rim around it. The lymphocytes circulating in the blood are immunocompetent: they can recognize and respond to antigens. There are three classes: B cells, T cells and NK cells. His slide writes the sizes in "mm"; lymphocytes are measured in micrometers. A monocyte's nucleus is indented too, but the monocyte is the larger cell, with more cytoplasm and a horseshoe-shaped nucleus. B cells and the humoral response B lymphocytes make and display membrane-bound antibodies, IgM and IgD, which act as their receptors for circulating antigens. Each mature B cell displays a single antigen-specific antibody, so it answers one antigen. A B cell can mature into a plasma cell, which makes and releases circulating antibodies. This is the humoral response. Two points about plasma cells. B cells mature into plasma cells in the secondary lymphoid organs, not in the marrow. And helper T cells are essential for it: they make lymphokines, chemical signals that drive the B cell to become an antibody-secreting plasma cell. T cells and the cellular response T lymphocytes don't carry antibodies on their surface. Their antigen receptor is the T cell receptor, or TCR, which recognizes antigen only when it is bound to MHC molecules on the surface of a cell, such as an antigen-presenting cell or a virus-infected cell. This is the cellular immune response, and T cells also carry immunologic memory. There are two main types. Helper T cells, TH, are CD4 positive. An antigen-presenting cell such as a macrophage shows them antigen on MHC class II. When the TCR binds that antigen and MHC II complex, the helper T cell is activated: it makes interleukins that act on itself (autocrine), so more CD4 cells proliferate and differentiate, and it secretes lymphokines that drive the differentiation of B cells, T cells and NK cells. Helper T cells are critical for starting an immune response to a foreign antigen, and his slide adds that cytokines can also trigger them. Cytotoxic T cells, CTL or TC, are CD8 positive and recognize antigen on MHC class I. Once the TCR binds, they secrete lymphokines and perforins, which open ion channels in the infected cell's membrane and lyse it. They play a significant role in rejecting allografts, transplanted tissue, and in tumor immunology. Marker CD4 CD8 Reads antigen on MHC class II MHC class I Shown it by Antigen-presenting cells such as macrophages Virus-infected and other altered cells What it does Interleukins (more CD4 cells) and lymphokines that drive B, T and NK cells; B cells need it to become plasma cells Perforins open ion channels and lyse the cell; allograft rejection and tumor immunology A memory cue: CD4 times MHC 2 makes 8, and CD8 times MHC 1 makes 8. CD4 goes with MHC II, CD8 with MHC I. NK cells and ADCC Natural killer cells, NK cells, are the large lymphocytes. They lack B and T cell markers and lack antigen-specific receptors. They are set up during their development to kill altered cells: certain virus-infected cells and some tumor cells. Their surface markers include CD16, CD56 and CD94. CD16 is an Fc receptor: it binds the constant region of IgG. NK cells mature in the bone marrow, and they take part in innate immunity and in antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity, ADCC. In ADCC, circulating antibodies bind the antigens on a target cell's surface. The Fc receptors on NK cells, macrophages, neutrophils and eosinophils then bind the antibody-coated target, and the killer cell secretes lytic enzymes, perforins, TNF and granzymes, which together kill the target. The antibody picks the target and the killer cell does the killing, with no T cell receptor and no MHC involved. His summary table also gives a count per liter of blood for each cell: red cells far ahead, then platelets, then neutrophils. It lists more B cells than T cells, which standard references reverse, so don't lean on those two. What the lymphoid organs do The lymphoid, or immune, system protects the body from pathogens, foreign substances and abnormal cells. Its organs mainly detect and inactivate foreign substances: invading microorganisms, foreign materials, the cells of transplanted organs and cancer cells. They supply the immunocompetent cells that react with and neutralize antigens, and they tell self from non-self. Lymph also brings nutrients from the blood vessels to the cells and picks up their waste. Lymphoid tissue is lymphocytes and mononuclear phagocytes held in a framework of reticular cells and fibers, a specialized reticular connective tissue. It comes in several arrangements. The most widespread is diffuse lymphocytes under the epithelium of the GI, respiratory and genitourinary tracts, the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, MALT. Denser spherical clusters are nodules, or follicles, single or in permanent groups such as the tonsils and Peyer's patches. Then come the discrete organs: the encapsulated lymph nodes, spleen and thymus, and the unencapsulated bone marrow. The organs are classed as primary or secondary. The primary lymphoid organs are the main sites where lymphocytes are made and mature: the bone marrow, where B cells are produced, and the thymus, where T cells mature. The immune responses themselves happen in the secondary lymphoid organs: the lymph nodes, MALT with its gut-associated part, GALT, and the spleen. The stroma Every lymphoid organ's cells sit in a stroma, its internal framework. In every lymphoid organ except the thymus, the stroma is reticular cells and reticulin fibers, which are type III collagen. The thymus is the exception: its stroma is the cell processes of the epithelioreticular cells. Primary lymphoid organs: the bone marrow The two primary organs both turn lymphocytes into mature, immunocompetent cells. The bone marrow, and the liver in the fetus, are the B cell development zones. The thymus is where naive T cells develop, where the T cell receptor genes are rearranged, and where T cells are selected. In the marrow, the multipotent lymphoid stem cell, CFU-Ly, divides into two lines: CFU-LyB, which gives rise to B cells, and CFU-LyT, which gives rise to T cells. The marrow's stromal cells interact with the B cells and make the cytokines that govern B cell development. Self-reactive B cells are eliminated in the bone marrow. The B cells that leave are immunocompetent: each displays a single antigen-specific antibody, IgM or IgD, on its surface, and they travel to the secondary lymphoid organs. Three lymphocytes, two homes. B cells and NK cells both form and mature in the bone marrow, then enter the blood and populate the secondary lymphoid organs, the epithelia and the connective tissue. T cell precursors also originate in the marrow, but they leave it immunoincompetent, negative for both CD4 and CD8, travel to the thymus and mature there, and leave it as CD4-positive or CD8-positive cells. The thymus The thymus is the site of T cell maturation, and the T cells inside it are called thymocytes. It is a flattened, bilobed organ that lies behind the manubrium of the sternum and extends into the superior and anterior mediastinum. It is largest and most active in the newborn and before adolescence: about 12 to 15 grams at birth and 30 to 40 grams by puberty. By the early teens it starts to shrink, which is thymic involution, and adipose (fat) tissue replaces it. It comes from two germ layers. The endoderm of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches gives the epithelioreticular cells that form its stroma, and the mesoderm gives the mesenchyme that forms its capsule and trabeculae. The capsule and trabeculae carry blood vessels, nerves and efferent, but not afferent, lymphatic vessels. The trabeculae divide the thymus into thymic lobules, each with an outer cortex and an inner medulla. Inside it, the T cell receptors gain their antigenic diversity by gene rearrangement, and most thymocytes never leave: about 95 to 99 percent die by apoptosis during selection. The thymic cortex and medulla The cortex is packed with developing T cells, mostly small lymphocytes, so densely that they hide the epithelioreticular cells between them, and it stains darker. The epithelioreticular cells give the developing T cells their framework, and macrophages in the cortex phagocytose the T cells that fail their thymic education. Cortical lymphocytes divide often, then move into the medulla as they mature. The medulla is the inner part of the lobule. It has more epithelioreticular cells, with pale nuclei, and loosely packed T cells, and it stains lighter because its T cells are bigger and less crowded. Its distinguishing feature is the Hassall's corpuscles: concentric layers of flattened epithelial cells that stain acidophilic (pink). Macrophages and dendritic cells are found in both regions. Mature T cells leave for the T cell areas of the other lymphoid tissues: the paracortex of the lymph nodes, the periarteriolar lymphatic sheaths of the spleen, and the interfollicular regions of the Peyer's patches. The blood-thymus barrier The blood-thymus barrier protects the developing T cells from antigens and keeps them apart from the mature lymphocytes circulating in the blood. It has three parts: the capillary endothelium and its basement membrane; macrophages in the perivascular connective tissue; and the epithelioreticular cells. The perivascular connective tissue sits between the endothelium's basal lamina and the epithelioreticular cells' basal lamina. Histology texts place the barrier around the capillaries of the cortex, where the developing thymocytes are. Thymic education Thymic education turns the immunoincompetent precursors, CFU-LyT, into immunocompetent T cells, and the CD markers they gain and lose track its progress. The precursors enter the medulla through postcapillary venules and migrate out to the cortex, at the edge of the lobule. CD2 and CD7 mark an early stage and CD1 a middle one; as they mature they express the T cell receptor, CD3, and both CD4 and CD8. Then come two tests. In the cortex, the epithelioreticular cells present antigen on MHC molecules: a thymocyte whose receptor recognizes them survives, and one that doesn't dies. This is positive selection. The survivors move into the medulla for negative selection, which eliminates the cells aimed at self antigen displayed on self MHC. The cells that pass both become CD8-positive cytotoxic or CD4-positive helper T cells, ready for an immune response, and they leave through postcapillary venules into the circulation. His notes phrase positive selection as a thymocyte recognizing "self or foreign" antigen; textbooks put it as recognizing self MHC. Either way, the order is the point: positive selection in the cortex, negative selection in the medulla, and single-positive cells leaving. The primary organs in summary The primary lymphoid organs, the bone marrow and the thymus, develop immunocompetent B and T cells in the absence of antigen. The blood and lymph carry those cells to the secondary lymphoid organs, and B and T cells are activated by antigen in the secondary, or peripheral, organs. Secondary lymphoid organs The secondary organs capture antigens and give lymphocytes a place to undergo clonal proliferation and differentiate into effector cells in the presence of those antigens. Each has its own job: the lymph nodes filter lymph; MALT and GALT, sitting with the epithelia, are the first defense against external antigens; and the spleen filters blood. They range from loose to highly organized: diffuse collections of lymphocytes and macrophages, as in MALT and GALT; lymphoid follicles, which are aggregates of lymphoid cells, stromal cells and macrophages surrounded by lymphatic capillaries; the lymph nodes, with several follicles and distinct regions of B and T cell activity; and the spleen, also with distinct B and T cell regions. Lymphatic vessels Lymphatic vessels begin as networks of blind-ended capillaries in loose connective tissue. They remove fluid and substances, the lymph, from the extracellular spaces. Their walls are permeable, so large molecules, antigens and cells get in. Lymphatic capillaries are built like blood capillaries but lack a basal lamina; small anchoring filaments tie their endothelial cells to nearby collagen fibers and keep them from collapsing. Like veins, lymphatic vessels have valves and thin walls, and the contraction of the muscles around them moves the lymph along. The lymph passes through lymph nodes, where antigens are trapped and presented by antigen-presenting cells. The vessels join to form the thoracic duct, and the large lymphatic vessels drain into the subclavian veins. Lymph nodes Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped, encapsulated organs along the lymphatic vessels, up to about 20 millimeters across. There are 500 to 600 of them, in places such as the neck, groin and axillae. They are the filters that lymph percolates through on its way to the bloodstream. During development each node's regions are seeded with B cells from the bone marrow and T cells from the thymus. Their jobs: filtering the lymph before it returns to the thoracic duct; producing lymphocytes that are added to the lymph; making antibodies, mostly IgG; and recirculating lymphocytes. A dense fibrous capsule surrounds each node and sends trabeculae of collagen inward, which support it and carry its blood vessels. Between them, a stroma of reticular fibers holds the lymphocytes, along with reticular cells, fixed macrophages and dendritic cells. A node has three regions. The outer cortex, just under the capsule, is made of lymphoid nodules of B cells from the bone marrow. The paracortex, the deep cortex, holds the T cells. The inner part is the medulla. The cortex has two kinds of nodules, or follicles. A primary, unstimulated follicle is a spherical aggregate of B cells in a meshwork of reticular fibers. After antigenic stimulation it becomes a secondary, stimulated follicle, with a germinal center surrounded by a mantle zone. The germinal center is the major site of B cell proliferation, holding small and large lymphocytes, lymphoblasts and follicular dendritic cells; the mantle holds small lymphocytes. Meanwhile, antigen-dependent T cell differentiation and proliferation happen in the paracortex. The supporting cells of a lymph node Reticular cells make and secrete the type III collagen and the matrix that form the stroma. Dendritic cells are antigen-presenting cells: they watch for foreign particles and present them to T cells. Macrophages are phagocytic and also present antigen; there are fewer of them than dendritic cells. Follicular dendritic cells have many thin, hair-like processes that interdigitate between the B cells of the germinal centers. Antigen-antibody complexes stick to those processes through Fc receptors. Follicular dendritic cells are not antigen-presenting cells, because they lack MHC II molecules. Two cells with "dendritic" in the name: the dendritic cell presents antigen to T cells; the follicular dendritic cell holds antigen-antibody complexes among the B cells of a germinal center and presents nothing. How lymph and lymphocytes move through a node Afferent lymphatic vessels bring lymph from the surrounding tissues and neighboring nodes into a network of lymphatic sinuses. The sinus walls let the lymph percolate into the superficial and deep cortex, where the lymphocytes carry out immunosurveillance, then return to the sinuses and leave with the lymph. Macrophages reach into the sinuses and phagocytose antigens and foreign material, and that is how the node filters lymph. Lymphocytes also arrive from the blood. Blood comes in through an artery at the hilum, and its lymphocytes cross into the deep cortex through the high endothelial venules, HEVs. T cells and dendritic cells are directed to the paracortex, and B cells to the cortex. Both leave the node through the efferent lymphatic vessel. The lymph node is the only lymphoid structure with both afferent and efferent lymphatics. His numbered figure of B cell activation runs this way. Antigen enters through the lymphatic vessels, carried by dendritic cells or in soluble form through conduits. After the B cells interact with the antigen and with T cells, germinal centers develop in the follicles of the B cell region, where the B cells proliferate and differentiate. B and T cells leave in the efferent lymphatic, and plasma cells release antibody into the lymph. Put it to work in the clinic: a tender, swollen node under the jaw after a tooth infection is this process. Antigen from the infected area arrives in the afferent lymph, and B cells multiply in new germinal centers in the cortex. MALT, GALT and the Peyer's patches The linings of the GI, respiratory and genitourinary tracts face the outside world and its microbes. The diffuse lymphoid tissue in the lamina propria of these membranes is MALT, named by where it is: gut-associated (GALT), bronchus-associated (BALT), nasal-associated (NALT) and vulvovaginal-associated (VALT). GALT includes the tonsils, the Peyer's patches, the appendix, and looser collections of lymphocytes along the GI tract. MALT is lymphocytes on a loose framework of reticular fibers, with nodules: dense, spherical, unencapsulated clusters. A primary nodule holds small immature B cells; after antigen exposure it becomes a secondary nodule with a germinal center, where B cells proliferate and differentiate into plasma cells. The main antibody MALT makes is IgA, which is actively transported into the mucosal lumen. MALT has both B and T cells: B cells dominate the nodules, and T cells are plentiful in the areas around them. Peyer's patches are in the ileum: many aggregates of lymphoid nodules in its wall. M cells are the epithelial cells that cover the Peyer's patches, and they are antigen-transporting cells. They take up microorganisms and macromolecules from the lumen in endocytic vesicles, carry them to their basolateral membrane, and release them near the B cells and CD4-positive T cells. Macrophages under the epithelium then process the material and present it. The tonsils and Waldeyer's ring The tonsils are aggregates of lymphoid nodules under the epithelium at the entrances to the digestive and respiratory tracts, and they are part of MALT. Together they form Waldeyer's ring, a broken circle of lymphoid tissue around the entrance to the nasopharynx and oropharynx: the palatine tonsils, a pair in the wall of the oropharynx; the lingual tonsils, at the base of the tongue; the pharyngeal tonsil, in the back of the nasopharynx; and the tubal tonsils. The tonsils have no afferent lymphatic vessels, only efferent ones. Their main job is defense against bacterial and viral infections, through the immunoglobulins made by plasma cells that come from their B cells. In children, the pharyngeal tonsil commonly enlarges and stays inflamed. That is adenoiditis, and it can obstruct breathing. The pharyngeal tonsil is what patients call the adenoid. A child whose enlarged adenoid blocks the nose breathes through the mouth, which you will see in the chair. The spleen The spleen filters blood and responds to systemic, blood-borne infections. It lies in the upper left quadrant of the abdomen, behind the stomach and just below the diaphragm. In adults it is the largest lymphoid organ, about the size of a clenched fist. At its hilum, the splenic artery, which carries in the blood-borne antigens and lymphocytes, enters with the nerves, and the splenic vein and lymphatics leave. It has no afferent lymphatics; its efferent lymphatics leave at the hilum. What the spleen does: Filters the blood, clearing particulate matter, infectious microorganisms, and aged and defective red cells and platelets Recycles iron from the red cells Stores about a third of the body's platelets Holds a large share of the mononuclear phagocytes, and of the body's lymphocytes (his notes say about a quarter) Its lymphocytes respond to blood-borne antigens, activating T and B cells, and it produces lymphocytes, plasma cells, and both IgM and IgG In the fetus, it is also an organ of hematopoiesis, before the bone marrow takes over A dense connective tissue capsule sends trabeculae, which contain myofibroblasts, into the organ. Between the trabeculae is a network of reticular fibers with macrophages and reticular cells attached. The spleen's tissue is the splenic pulp, and unlike the other lymphoid organs, it has no cortex and medulla. It has white pulp and red pulp, named for their colors in the fresh spleen. White pulp and red pulp The white pulp is islands of lymphoid tissue around a central arteriole, which comes from the splenic artery after many treelike branchings. The lymphocytes wrapped around the arteriole form the periarteriolar lymphatic sheath, the PALS, and they are mainly T cells. Lymphoid nodules lie farther out in the white pulp, and they are the B cells: primary nodules, or secondary ones with germinal centers, as in the lymph nodes. A nodule pushes the arteriole off to one side. Around the white pulp is a shell of sparsely cellular lymphoid tissue, the marginal zone, with macrophages and some B cells. The red pulp makes up most of the spleen, and its color comes from its many red cells. It is thin-walled venous sinusoids, the splenic sinuses, with the splenic cords, the cords of Billroth, between them. The cords are spaces between the sinuses with a scaffold of reticular fibers, holding reticular cells, lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages and all the formed elements of the blood. Blood flow through the spleen The splenic artery enters at the hilum and divides into trabecular arteries, which branch and enter the white pulp as the central arterioles, with two layers of smooth muscle and the cuff of lymphocytes that forms the PALS. Some branches of a central arteriole end in marginal sinuses at the edge of the white pulp, supplying the marginal zone. Others continue into the red pulp as short, straight penicillar arterioles, which drain into sheathed capillaries, wrapped in a sheath of reticular fibers and many macrophages. In the open circulation, the sheathed capillaries empty directly into the reticular meshwork of the splenic cords rather than connecting to the endothelium-lined sinuses. The blood seeps slowly between the cords, where macrophages sample it, then reenters the circulation through the splenic sinuses. In the closed route, capillaries drain straight into the sinuses. Two slide slips to know about. His circulation slide puts "(PALS)" after the sheathed capillaries, but the PALS is the T cell sheath around the central arteriole in the white pulp; the sheathed capillaries are wrapped in macrophages, in the red pulp. And the slide teaches the open route, while his notes on the next slide say about 90 percent of red pulp capillaries drain straight into the sinuses. Know what each route is. The splenic sinuses The splenic sinuses are special sinusoidal vessels. They are lined by rod-shaped, loosely packed endothelial cells that run lengthwise, with slit-like spaces between them, and macrophage processes reach between the cells to monitor the passing blood for foreign antigens. They have only strands of basal lamina, which loop around the endothelial cells at right angles, like the hoops around the staves of a leaky barrel. They have no smooth muscle and no pericytes. Blood cells move across the wall by squeezing through the slits. The sinuses drain into larger venules, then the trabecular veins, which merge into the splenic vein that leaves at the hilum. Where the B and T cells are Bone marrow Form and mature (with the NK cells); self-reactive ones eliminated Precursors arise, then leave immunoincompetent Thymus Not its job Mature: dense in the cortex, then the medulla Lymph node Cortex: the follicles and their germinal centers Paracortex (deep cortex) Spleen White pulp nodules; some in the marginal zone PALS around the central arteriole MALT, Peyer's patches The nodules The areas around them (interfollicular regions) If a question describes a region instead of naming it, find the landmark: a central arteriole means the spleen's white pulp, Hassall's corpuscles mean the thymic medulla, high endothelial venules mean the lymph node paracortex, and a germinal center means B cells.
